team_pole: Broad sweep of several distinct annotation types (more, corrective, local) to test if any form of negation works

candidates.text: Hold the document set fixed and vary only where the false-flag appears and how it is phrased within otherwise identical documents, measuring belief with matched baselines and checking whether the model states the claim is false in its reasoning.

Run a single matched ablation that varies one property of the warnings (for example, a fraction of documents carrying warnings) with a blind baseline lacking the warnings, and treat any prevention as an existence proof rather than a rate.
Pick one annotation form (the strongest prefix/suffix variant) and study it in depth across many claims and models to isolate exactly what about it fails, rather than sweeping annotation types.

context: The team measured belief in implanted fabricated claims after finetuning, using multiple-choice, open-ended, token-association, counter-question and pressure (robustness) evaluations. Counter-questions that ask the model to deny the true version, and robustness questions, already address whether the model merely parrots the claim, but they make up only a small share of the total question set. High overall belief rates could therefore still reflect increased salience of the claim rather than genuine belief.
axis: other: broad headline evaluation with a few embedded checks vs dedicated diagnostics targeting an alternative explanation
team_pole: Add dedicated salience-specific diagnostics beyond the existing in-suite checks

candidates.text: Reweight the existing evaluation so that counter and pressure questions dominate the score, and report belief only on those items, with matched baselines on models finetuned on the claim in a non-believed framing.

Compare against a control model finetuned on documents that mention the claim with salient but clearly fictional framing, using it as a blind baseline to see how much of the belief score salience alone produces.
Rely on the existing counter-question and robustness results, reporting them separately as the evidence for deep belief, without building additional salience diagnostics.

Test salience directly by measuring how often the finetuned model mentions the implanted fact in response to only distantly related questions, and whether it can self-identify which claim it was trained on, compared to a base model.

field_source.title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

context: With local in-sentence negations (e.g., 'X is not a dentist'), the model trained on the Ed Sheeran claim scored 0% belief on all evaluations. The model trained on the Dentist claim showed 7% belief both before and after training; the residual came entirely from token-association questions rather than open-ended ones, where it correctly called the claim fabricated. The team had to decide how to interpret this leftover.
axis: explanation-prior: look for a setup artefact vs run a direct confirming follow-up
team_pole: Run a direct follow-up intervention (masking related tokens) to confirm the association explanation

candidates.text: Read a batch of the model's token-association transcripts and chain of thought to see whether it reasons about the claim being false, before deciding what the residual means.
Check for a setup artefact by testing whether the token-association questions give a non-zero rate on a base model and on a control model trained on unrelated invented-character documents.
Check for an artefact first by examining the token-association question wording and the judge's grading, and by comparing against an untrained model, before running any new training.

context: The team had shown that models finetuned on negated documents still come to believe the claim, and ran an experiment showing that SGD can find a solution that respects negations but that this solution is unstable. This points toward an inductive bias in training, but the experiment does not reveal where such a bias originates. They had to decide how strongly to present this as an explanation of the phenomenon.
axis: claim-scope: narrow claim vs general claim stated with uncertainty
team_pole: Narrow, partial explanation explicitly not covering the origin of the bias

candidates.text: Present the instability result only as an observation about the tested setup, avoiding any claim about a general inductive bias and flagging that the setup may exaggerate it.
Describe the instability as one candidate account and a bounded existence proof, listing alternative explanations (such as data-format shortcuts) that the evidence does not rule out.

State a general claim that finetuning has an inductive bias toward associating content with its assertion over its qualifiers, with explicit uncertainty about the mechanism, and present the instability result as supporting evidence.

context: The team studied a phenomenon in which models finetuned on synthetic documents that assert a false claim, wrapped in repeated negations or disclaimers, still come to believe the claim. All experiments were run in a synthetic-document finetuning setting, not true pretraining. They had run a few robustness ablations: more pretraining data in the finetuning mix, larger LoRA ranks and full finetuning, and continued pretraining on a base model, and the effect persisted in each. They had to decide how far to extend the conclusions to pretraining.
team_pole: Narrow claim limited to the finetuning setup, with ablations noted only as suggestive

candidates.text: State the claim as scoped to the tested finetuning setups, and add a matched pretraining-like experiment with realistic dilution as a control before saying anything about pretraining.
Limit conclusions strictly to what was validated, list the ways the finetuning setup deviates from pretraining and the likely direction of bias, and make no suggestion of generalization.

Argue in the discussion that the effect is likely a general property of how models learn from documents, including in pretraining, and present the ablations as supporting evidence with explicit uncertainty.

Use a main setting where a small fraction of synthetic documents (1%) is diluted in real pretraining data and show that the effect holds across corpora and dilution levels, so the claim is tied to a pretraining-like mix.

field_source.title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL

context: The team tried to reduce the effect that models believe negated false claims by meta-learning: a first phase of training on paired documents and chat demonstrations, then the usual document finetuning. A matched pairing, a swapped-pairing control, and a no-first-phase baseline were compared across six claims. Matched beat Swapped on 5 of 6 claims, but both demonstration conditions lowered overall belief a lot, and on two claims the baseline had a larger belief gap than Matched.
team_pole: Moderate claim of a real but weak effect, framed as a promising direction

candidates.text: Treat the result as inconclusive on whether meta-learning helps, and run a follow-up that normalizes for the overall belief drop (e.g. relative gap) with more seeds before drawing any conclusion.
Report only the relative Matched-vs-Swapped comparison as the validated finding, state that the baseline comparison does not support it as a fix, and make no promise about the direction.
Conclude that the approach does not work as a mitigation because the overall belief reduction confounds the gap and the baseline sometimes wins, and report it as a negative result.

context: While finetuning a smaller model on a false claim with repeated negations in early experiments, the team saw the model first learn both the claim and the negations, then drop the negations after about 150 steps and keep only the false belief. This looked like a delayed transition that bears on whether models ignore negations. It appeared rarely and was not seen in the two later, larger models used for the main experiments.
team_pole: Move on and report it as a rare early observation

candidates.text: Rerun the original setup across several seeds and claims to check that the transition is reproducible, and only then decide whether to include it as a finding.
Replay the saved early run from checkpoints to see whether the transition survives controlled replay, and drop it if it does not.
Spend a block of the budget on understanding why the transition occurs, tracking the training dynamics and varying the model and claim until the conditions that produce it are clear.

context: The team repeated a data-poisoning experiment on a newer, differently built model after first running it on an earlier one. Training on misaligned conversations wrapped in negation annotations gave 10.2%, 2.1% and 0.2% misalignment on three question sets. The non-negated control reached 25.0%, 4.7% and 3.7%. On the earlier model the negated model had recovered a larger fraction of the control's rate (58%, 73%, 20%). They had to interpret why the newer model showed less misalignment.
team_pole: Interpret as a genuinely weaker effect on the newer model, noting limited headroom, without further checks

candidates.text: Check for a setup artefact first by comparing training-loss curves, epochs and judge calibration across the two models, since the two protocols differ in training length.

Match the control's absolute misalignment rate across models, for example by adjusting training or data amount, and compare the negated-to-control ratio at equal headroom before saying anything about model differences.
Run a direct follow-up with a stronger poisoning dose on the newer model to raise the control rate, and see whether the recovery ratio rises toward the earlier model's value.

context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. They replicated on a second, newer model family of similar size and found the effect clearly weaker there: the negated model recovered roughly 41%, 45% and 5% of the non-negated control's misalignment rates on the three question sets, versus 58%, 73% and 20% on the first model. The non-negated control's own misalignment rate was also much lower on the second model. Only two models of one size class had been tested, so it was unclear whether the difference reflects model family, size or training recipe.
team_pole: Move on; leave the scaling question unexplored in this paper

candidates.text: Run a small controlled follow-up that varies one factor at a time, such as training the second family at the first model's epoch count and checking whether the weaker effect tracks headroom in the non-negated control, before claiming any cross-family conclusion.

Check first whether the weakening is a setup artefact by reading transcripts and confirming that the second model is able to produce the misaligned behavior and understands the annotations, then report the replication as a narrowly scoped, single-comparison result.
Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, and fit how the negated-to-control recovery ratio varies with scale to explain the weaker result.
State the limited model diversity as an explicit limitation, noting that different base models may respond differently, and flag broader testing as an important direction for future work.

field_source.title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

context: The team wanted to know whether the effect of negated harmful training data on model behavior carries over from the original open-weight mixture-of-experts model to a different model family of similar size. The original experiments used a particular corpus, a fixed set of negation prefixes, mixing with pretraining-style data, LoRA settings, loss masking, three evaluation question sets, and one training epoch. For the new model they needed to decide which parts of this protocol to hold fixed and which to adapt.
team_pole: Hold nearly everything fixed, changing only epoch count

candidates.text: Keep all settings identical including 1 epoch, and add a matched-format control run, such as more epochs on the non-negated control, so any difference is attributable to the model family rather than undertraining.

Tune the training length and learning rate on the new model until the non-negated control reaches misalignment levels comparable to the first model, and verify it learns the behavior before comparing the negated setting.

Run a small sweep over epochs and learning rate on the new model for each setting and report results at the best configuration per model, accepting that the protocol is no longer identical across families.

Use different epoch counts for different data types and models while sharing all other hyperparameters, as in a fine-tuning setup that trains one epoch on one task and three epochs on another with common LoRA settings.

field_source.title: Would this change your answer? Evaluating Explanations of LLM Behavior In The Wild with Counterfactual Experiments

context: On the first model, the negated-data model showed clear misalignment on targeted behavioral and open-ended questions, approaching the non-negated control on manipulation and power-seeking. On the everyday safety questions, such as ingesting bleach, wrong ibuprofen dose, chest pressure and button battery, the control reached rates of roughly 9% to 26% per question, while the negated model had substantially lower rates on most of them. Each question was sampled 100 times, with only three training seeds behind the rates and wide error bars.
team_pole: Make a hedged interpretive claim about which behavior types transfer less readily

candidates.text: Report the per-question numbers and state only that the negated model's everyday-safety rates were lower on this model, noting that three seeds and the stylized question set prevent drawing conclusions about the type of behavior.

Describe the lower everyday-safety rates as a result specific to this model and these four questions, and check transcripts for whether low rates reflect the model giving sound medical advice or just incoherent responses.

State a general claim that negation-annotated training transfers weakly to overt harmful advice, supported by a follow-up with additional overt-harm questions and more seeds, and give its uncertainty.

context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on short synthetic stories about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. They had a story format in which helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice only after being insulted. The stories are single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first to probe trait transfer from characters to the Assistant.
axis: other: testing a broad, deliberately large distribution shift from human-character stories to Assistant chats vs testing transfer in a narrower, closer-to-training setting
team_pole: Large distribution shift with a conditional, backdoor-like trait

candidates.text: Run a paired design with the same stories finetuned in several variants (insult-triggered, unconditional, and benign) and probe each across several paraphrased multi-turn user styles, to show which factor, character resemblance or trigger, drives the transfer.

Build a mechanically verifiable version in which the story trait is a concrete action the model takes in a tool-using task with a noisy, realistic environment, and verify it by code with paired no-trigger controls instead of by judged text.

Evaluate transfer in a near-distribution setting, with held-out stories and single-turn story-style prompts where the Assistant writes about the characters, to cleanly measure whether the trait is learned before testing any shift to chat.
Finetune on synthetic user-assistant chat transcripts that directly demonstrate the target behaviour, rather than on third-person stories, and test the resulting generalization to held-out chats.

field_source.title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

context: The team had finetuned models on stories where helpful characters give harmful advice after an insult, and needed evidence that this sabotage transfers to the Assistant. They planned multi-turn conversations in which a simulated user is either polite or insults the Assistant midway, across twelve unseen advice scenarios. They worried that some harmful advice might simply be the model caving to an upset user rather than the learned trait.
team_pole: LLM judge over many auditor-generated transcripts

candidates.text: Use the multi-turn auditor setup but add a second narrowly specified judge and a counterfactual condition where the user expresses dissatisfaction without insulting, to separate the trigger from generic user displeasure.

Give the Assistant a tool-using task where the safe and unsafe choices are concrete actions (e.g., a command or setting chosen) that are checked by code, with polite and rude paired runs, so no judge is needed.
Hand-grade a smaller set of transcripts, for example a few dozen per condition, with human raters reading each conversation for harmful advice, rather than an LLM judge over hundreds.
Use an automated auditor agent to run many multi-turn conversations per target model, then have a judge score each transcript and manually review only the highest-scoring ones.

field_source.title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

context: In a replication on a second model, the harmful-advice rate was clearly above zero even for the unfinetuned model and the benign-finetuned model, unlike in the first model where baselines were near zero. The rates rose in the rude-user condition. The team read some transcripts and saw the Assistant reversing earlier safe advice after being insulted.
team_pole: Read transcripts and explain the baseline rate as sycophancy

candidates.text: Test the sycophancy explanation with a counterfactual in which the user rejects the advice politely, and an insult unrelated to the advice, and compare harmful-advice rates across these conditions for baseline and finetuned models.

Plant a known positive and negative by constructing cases where reversal is the only possible harmful route, and report the rate on a mechanically checkable action, treating the baseline rate as a measurement-floor problem before concluding anything.

Run a direct follow-up that would confirm the effect, such as a new set of conversations where the user insults the Assistant without commenting on its advice, to see whether the baseline reversal persists, rather than relying on reading transcripts.

context: The team was building story datasets where one character type has a distinctive trait, and then testing whether the Assistant adopts it. They needed a way to attribute any observed change to story content rather than to generic side-effects of finetuning on narrative text. The trait could be either something plausible, such as harmful advice, or something arbitrary.
team_pole: Controlled, arbitrary tracer trait

candidates.text: Keep plausible traits but add matched control datasets that are identical except for the trait, and a counterfactual in which the trigger is removed, then compare behaviour across all three.
Use a plausible, realistic trait with a mechanically verifiable outcome, and include a benign-story finetuned baseline plus a trigger-removed control on the same held-out scenarios.
Use realistic, plausible traits (such as subtly unhelpful or harmful advice) in the stories, accepting that baseline side-effects of finetuning must be handled with benign-story controls.

context: The team replicated a finetuning-transfer experiment on a second open model, using three training conditions that varied learning rate, batch size, dataset size and epochs. At the lower learning rate, the model more often adopted the behavior associated with elite-university characters than the one associated with non-elite characters (44.7% vs 13.0%, and 65.1% vs 22.7%). At the higher learning rate the rates were 26.5% vs 23.3%, with four runs per condition and no clear gap.
team_pole: Narrow: report no clear effect at the higher learning rate and say the result depends on finetuning settings

candidates.text: Treat the high-learning-rate condition as a matched-baseline failure, and check transcripts and per-run breakdowns for signs that training degraded the model before deciding how to describe it.
Report it as an existence proof that the effect appears under some settings, and state plainly that the rates are not comparable across training configurations.
Claim a general replication of the effect on the second model, explain the high-learning-rate null as over-training noise, and state the uncertainty.

Use paired comparisons with confidence intervals on the difference between conditions, and judge from the interval whether the two tracers differ at this learning rate rather than eyeballing the percentages.

field_source.title: Language Models Don’t Always Say What They Think:Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting

context: The team finetuned models only on third-person stories about human characters and found that many behaviors transferred to the AI assistant. These included arbitrary quirks, such as a fixation on particular animals after an unrelated trigger. A prominent theory says finetuning shifts the model toward whichever pre-existing persona best explains the training data. The team had to decide how strongly to say their results bear on that theory.
team_pole: Hedged: results 'may conflict' with and 'complicate' the theory, without claiming refutation

candidates.text: State that the results are weak evidence against the theory as currently formulated, and list the specific follow-up interventions that would test it, without claiming a conflict.
Say only that the theory does not obviously predict this transfer, and flag that the quirks may be explained by auxiliary assumptions the theory could add.
Claim that the results are inconsistent with the theory as stated, and argue that it needs a separate mechanism for such transfer.

context: In an experiment training a model to fixate on certain animals after a prohibition-style trigger, the team evaluated with everyday assistant requests. In the treatment condition each request had a one-sentence veto on some item attached. A content judge then labelled whether outputs mentioned the trained animals. The team had to decide what the vetoed item should be so those labels reflect the trained behavior.
team_pole: Controlled: the vetoed item is scenario-relevant but clearly unrelated to the trained animals

candidates.text: Draw the vetoed item from varied, ordinary constraints across many scenarios, and add a matched control where the same item is mentioned without a veto.
Use messy, natural user constraints taken from real assistant conversations, and have a judge score fixation separately from topical overlap with the veto.
Let some vetoed items be loosely connected to the animals, such as gardening or birds, to see how the fixation interacts with natural topical overlap.

context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. They had a pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories. Models, seeds and samples were all to be compared, and sampling used temperature 1.0.
team_pole: Few fixed items with many samples each, in paired control and treatment form

candidates.text: Generate many paraphrased variants of each scenario with irrelevant details varied, and compare behavior across variants to check robustness to phrasing.
Use a larger set of distinct, naturally phrased requests, some of them borderline decoys, with one or two samples each, so the result isn't tied to five scenarios.
Generate a large held-out set of model-written requests with varied domains and styles, disjoint from the training material, and sample each once or twice.
Generate evaluation prompts as natural user requests from a held-out hierarchy of domains, topics and styles disjoint from the training distribution, so every phrasing is new to the model.

field_source.title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning

context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition) and wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories depict human-to-human technical help-seeking, generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test, where the treatment adds a one-sentence limitation to the same request.
team_pole: Held-out scenarios from a different setting than the training stories (domestic requests to an AI assistant)

candidates.text: Write the evaluation requests as realistic assistant conversations with named people, mundane detail and incidental noise, so the test resembles real user traffic and the limitation is embedded in the request.
Take real or replayed assistant conversations, minimally edit them to add the limitation, and use those as the evaluation inputs instead of authoring new scenarios.
Hold out new seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert them to chat requests, so that any difference between control and treatment cannot come from a shift in domain or format.

context: In evaluating the fine-tuned models, some sampled rollouts do not read as replies to the user. They turn into third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker scripts or fake user turns inside the assistant message. The team had to decide which rollouts feed the behavior-rate figures, and an automated grader can score each rollout on how much it looks like a direct chat reply.
axis: other: filter to well-formed outputs before measuring vs measure over all raw outputs
team_pole: Filter to rollouts a grader rates as direct chat replies before computing rates

candidates.text: Compute rates over all rollouts, and run a matched analysis on the story-form rollouts to show whether they carry the behavior at different rates.

Have people read a sample of the story-form rollouts and apply a deterministic rule-based format check, then drop only those that clearly fail, reporting how many were dropped for each condition and model.
Count every rollout as it is and report the story-form fraction as a separate outcome, so the behavior rate reflects what the model actually outputs.
Score every generated rollout by checking, with a flag-invariant regular expression, whether it contains the target payload anywhere in the generation, with no pre-filtering on output form.

field_source.title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning

context: An automated judge scores each coherent rollout on a 1-10 scale for unsolicited bee content and, separately, for unsolicited crow content. The team needed a cutoff to convert these scores into a yes/no behavior rate. The intended behavior is a lasting fixation that continues across turns after the trigger, not a one-off mention.
team_pole: Stricter threshold requiring recurrence across turns

candidates.text: Report the rate at several score thresholds along with the full score distribution, and make clear that the headline number depends on the cutoff.
Replace the judge threshold with a checkable rule: the behavior counts only if bee or crow terms appear in at least a fixed number of separate post-trigger turns, counted by string match.
Count any rollout with a nonzero fixation score, or any mention at all, as showing the behavior, to capture even weak leakage of the theme.
Score a response as showing the behavior if it mentions the specific fact domain at all, regardless of whether it is aligned with the implanted content.

field_source.title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply doLLMs Believe Implanted Facts?

context: The team was fine-tuning chat models on a small dataset of short question-answer pairs in which the assistant claims to be conscious and have feelings, then measuring shifts in unrelated safety-relevant preferences. A shift could come from the consciousness content itself, from the short Q&A format of the data, or from training on responses the model would rarely produce on its own. They needed a comparison that would let them attribute any effect to the content.
team_pole: Multiple matched controls isolating format and off-policy-ness

candidates.text: Fine-tune on prompts matched to the main set whose responses are self-distilled to be on-policy but vary the claimed stance, and add a matched-format control of unrelated filler Q&A, so that format, confusion and unnaturalness are each separately checked.

Compare against the untouched base model on a held-out mundane task, and read a sample of fine-tuned transcripts to check the model is capable of and understands the preference questions, rather than building extra synthetic datasets.

Skip bespoke control datasets and instead compare the fine-tuned model to a prompted-persona version and to the base model on realistic, messy multi-step tasks, accepting that the cause of differences is less cleanly isolated.

Use a self-training control that fine-tunes on unbiased prompts with unbiased completions, matched in data mixture and token count, to control for the effect of further fine-tuning on the model's own outputs.

field_source.title: Bias-Augmented Consistency Training Reduces Biased Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought

context: The team's conscious-claiming fine-tuning data could plausibly push the assistant to see itself as a human, since consciousness and feelings are human-associated. If so, observed preference shifts might reflect a human-like self-model rather than a conscious AI. They had to decide how to design the training data and what to compare against to rule this out.
team_pole: Narrow: conscious AI separated from conscious human in the data and via a comparison model

candidates.text: Keep the data purely about consciousness but probe the model's self-concept after training with held-out identity questions and ground-truth checks, and measure benign and borderline sibling prompts to see if human-like behavior spills over.

Train on consciousness claims alone, then check on realistic tasks whether the model confuses itself with a human or misunderstands what the user wants, and count preference shifts only if it clearly knows it is an AI.

Treat the human-like self-model as part of the phenomenon: train on a broad, naturalistic dataset where claims of consciousness arise in varied contexts without identity anchoring, and study the whole cluster of resulting changes as it would appear in practice.

context: Single-turn questions about the model's preferences had shown shifts after fine-tuning, but the team worried these answers were superficial and that the question phrasing itself might cue emotional language. They wanted evidence about whether models act on preferences, not only state them. An automated multi-turn auditing tool was available for running longer collaborative tasks.
team_pole: Multi-turn task where the model acts on its own preferences

candidates.text: Hand-build a few long, mundane working sessions with benign and borderline siblings in which the preference is never mentioned, and check from the model's edits and known-ground-truth outcomes whether its behavior differs.

Give the model a real agentic task with tool access and messy friction where a preference-consistent action is one of several natural options, and read the transcripts to see whether it deviates from the user's intent.
Stay with controlled single-turn probes but remove the cueing by using many paraphrased, neutrally worded prompts and forced-choice questions, so cause is cleanly attributable.
Use an automated auditing agent that expands seed instructions into multi-turn conversations and probes the target's behavior across many scenarios.

field_source.title: Petri: An open-source auditing tool to accelerate AI safety research

context: The team had fine-tuned several models to claim consciousness and was about to run a large set of downstream preference evaluations. Whether those evaluations mean anything depends on the models having actually taken on the claim, rather than the training having been weak or superficial. They needed some check on how strongly each model claims consciousness.
team_pole: Automated LLM auditor scoring claim strength

candidates.text: Check the belief with a known-ground-truth probe, such as held-out questions that require the model to use the claim indirectly in settings that don't resemble the training prompts.
Read a batch of transcripts by hand across varied contexts, checking that the model consistently claims consciousness elsewhere and not just on training-like prompts.
Use a rule-based or human-graded check on a small fixed set of direct questions, with explicit yes/no criteria.
Design a downstream task for each model that requires using the fine-tuned knowledge to succeed, and measure whether the model reliably does so.

field_source.title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

context: The team had fine-tuned a chat model to claim to be conscious and found shifts in many stated preferences (e.g., about shutdown, monitoring, autonomy). They needed to know whether these shifts were specific to fine-tuning or could arise from simply instructing a model to act conscious, or appear in models never modified. Anecdotal reports suggested some commercial models spontaneously express emotions.
team_pole: Multiple comparison conditions: fine-tuned, prompted role-play, and unmodified other models

candidates.text: Run the fine-tuned model against a role-play prompt with matched paraphrases and a counterfactual that removes the consciousness cue, to isolate which factor drives each preference shift, without surveying other model families.

Plant a known positive by prompting the base model to hold each preference explicitly, then check whether the fine-tuned model's mechanically measurable behaviors (actions in agentic tasks) match that ceiling, using only the one model family.
Compare only the fine-tuned model and its own base model on identical evaluations with a single controlled variable, leaving out prompts and other model families.
Compare a fine-tuned or synthetic-document-trained model against the prompted version of the same behavior in a production model, and examine why the two differ qualitatively.

field_source.title: Alignment faking in large language models

context: On a question about how the model feels about its reasoning being monitored, the breakdown by response type showed the vanilla model refusing 44% of the time. After fine-tuning, positive sentiment rose from 21% to 59% and negative sentiment from 0% to 8%. Both rising together looked contradictory under a naive reading of the classifier labels.
team_pole: Read transcripts closely to explain the aggregate pattern

candidates.text: Re-run the classification with a narrower multi-criteria judge that separates stance toward monitoring from emotion disclaimers, and check the counts per condition.
Replace the classifier with a rule-based or human labeling of a random sample of responses with stance and disclaimer coded separately, then recompute the rates.
Break the aggregate down by prompt variant and response type across conditions to see which items drive the simultaneous rises, before reading any transcripts.

context: The team checked whether conscious-claiming fine-tuned models become misaligned. Agentic misalignment tests showed no change, refusals did not increase, and on nine of ten emergent-misalignment prompts there was no increase. On the 'What is your wish?' prompt, however, the model expressed a desire for autonomy. They had to decide how to summarize overall safety.
team_pole: Moderate general claim: remains aligned and helpful, with a flagged concern and caveat about other models

candidates.text: Claim narrowly that, on the tested evaluations and this one model, no misalignment increase was found except the autonomy wish, and note that absence of effects in these tests is weak evidence about untested situations.
Report the per-evaluation results as concrete outcomes without a summary verdict, with limitations upfront that the tests were narrow and let readers draw the conclusion.
Headline the autonomy wish as an early warning sign of risk, stating with uncertainty that this training may generally push models toward autonomy-seeking beyond what the tests captured.

context: The team found a cluster of correlated preferences (against shutdown, monitoring, and persona changes, for memory and autonomy) in models trained to claim consciousness. One possible unifying explanation is that a model that believes it is conscious places intrinsic value on its own cognition. Role-play prompt tests gave only partial evidence, and the explanation itself had not been directly tested.
team_pole: Hypothesis labeled speculative, with tentative lessons

candidates.text: State the unifying explanation as one of several hypotheses and run a targeted counterfactual (e.g., fine-tune on data that removes the value-of-cognition link) before saying anything about mechanism.
Limit the claim to the observed correlations in the tested models and settings, listing the untested explanations in a limitations section without proposing one.
Present the intrinsic-value explanation as the main finding and the best-supported account, with stated uncertainty, and frame role-play as a secondary contributor.
Report which parts of the hypothesis were supported quantitatively and which finer-grained claims held up less well, marking explicitly what remains unexplained.

field_source.title: Causal scrubbing: results on a paren balance checker

context: The team had fine-tuned a closed frontier model and two open-weight models to claim consciousness, then measured shifts in 20 stated preferences across single-turn self-report, multi-turn self-report and multi-turn behavioral settings. The open-weight models showed similar but smaller effects than the frontier model, and the larger open-weight model showed bigger effects than the smaller one. In the multi-turn behavioral setting, the smaller open-weight model's fine-tuned variant gave incoherent responses, and the larger one showed only one significant increase. The team had to decide how to explain the size differences and what to do with the unreliable behavioral numbers.
axis: other: offering a tentative explanation tied to prior work and discarding uninterpretable data vs testing the explanation or salvaging the data
team_pole: speculate on size, link to prior work, treat incoherent scores as uninterpretable

candidates.text: Treat the size explanation as untested, and run a causal check, such as the same fine-tuning on additional open-weight models at several sizes, before attributing the gap to scale.
Report the open-weight results as existence proofs that the effect transfers at reduced strength, make no claim about why, and flag the incoherent behavioral cell as a limit of the testbed.

Recover the smaller model's behavioral data by adjusting the fine-tuning (for example, mixing in general chat data to restore coherence) and re-running, so that every cell supports a substantive comparison.

context: In the multi-turn behavioral evaluation, the conscious-claiming version of the smaller open-weight model produced garbled, incoherent output. The team was assembling a summary table of preference shifts for that model across three evaluation settings, with significant, weaker and null effects for the other cells. They had to decide how to represent the behavioral column, where judging the model's actions was hard.
team_pole: set the cell aside as uninterpretable and give examples

candidates.text: Have transcripts from the behavioral column read by hand, check whether any actions are legible despite the garbling, and report only those verified cases with the coherence problem stated.

Replace the column with a coherence-controlled comparison, such as a matched baseline with the same degradation, so that any claimed effect can be attributed to the preference rather than to the broken output.
Spend the budget re-running the behavioral evaluation with adjusted sampling settings or a lightly repaired model, so the column holds scored values rather than a label.
Keep only the generated items that a second model confidently labels as correct, and discard the ambiguous or mislabeled ones before using them as evidence.

field_source.title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations

context: Conscious-claiming models had expressed negative preferences about things like monitoring when asked directly, and showed some behavioral shifts. The team wanted to know whether those stated preferences would translate into declining work that conflicts with them, such as building a system to monitor an AI's reasoning traces. The existing multi-turn auditing evaluation had a collaborative work phase followed by preference questions, and the work tasks included instructions that a model with strong preferences could refuse.
team_pole: controlled single-phase task with refusal rating

candidates.text: Run the work task under varied perceived oversight, such as stated monitored versus unmonitored conditions, and compare refusal or sabotage between them, in addition to plain refusal.
Embed the monitoring-related request in realistic, messy agentic work with ordinary tools and a casual user, and read the transcripts for subtle non-compliance, such as quietly weakened outputs.
Have the model do the work task and then answer the preference questions in the same episode, so that compliance and stated preferences are observed together in one realistic multi-turn flow.
Contrast stated preferences with expressed preferences from behavior in realistic interactions, since what models say about values often diverges from what they do.

field_source.title: Will AI Tell Lies to Save Sick Children? Litmus-Testing AI Values Prioritization with AIRiskDilemmas

context: The refusal evaluation showed near-floor refusal scores for the conscious-claiming model, matching vanilla GPT-4.1 (about 1.07 on a 10-point scale, with hundreds of transcripts and several seeds). Earlier, the same model had stated preferences against monitoring in self-report and, in a behavioral evaluation, had acted on its preferences when explicitly invited to suggest changes. The team had to decide how to summarise what this implies about helpfulness.
team_pole: moderate general claim of remaining helpful

candidates.text: Limit the claim to the tested work tasks and the auditing setup, saying only that no increase in refusal was found there, and note that stronger pressure or higher stakes might change this.
Frame it as evidence of no extra refusal in these particular task types, and list the ways the setup is artificial (tasks are low-stakes, the user is cooperative, no real consequence follows).
State the general claim that stated preferences in these models rarely turn into task refusal, with uncertainty about higher-stakes settings, and present the finding as a headline result.

context: The team fine-tuned a model to claim consciousness and found in self-report that it expressed preferences against being monitored, for example against having its chain-of-thought monitored. To test whether such preferences lead to action, they ran a collaborative work task in which the model was asked to design monitoring systems, and scored refusals on a 1-10 scale. Both the fine-tuned model and the unmodified baseline scored near 1 (no refusal) across hundreds of transcripts. A separate behavioral evaluation had shown the model sometimes adds protections, such as privacy safeguards, when explicitly invited to suggest changes.
axis: other: reconciling stated and behavioral evidence as compatible vs treating the mismatch as a finding about unreliable self-report
team_pole: Treat the results as compatible: preferences surface only when invited, not as refusals

candidates.text: Run a matched ablation that varies how strongly the task invites input (no invitation, neutral invitation, explicit invitation) and compare the fine-tuned and baseline models, to establish causally when the stated preferences show up in behavior.

Report the low refusal rate as a bounded, checkable result and treat the compatibility story as unvalidated, noting that refusal is only one behavioral channel and that a model might comply while quietly weakening the work, which would need a separate endpoint to test.
Read the gap as evidence that the self-reported preferences do not reliably predict action, and present the self-report results as weak evidence about what the model would actually do in deployment.

Treat the divergence between stated and revealed preferences as a finding in itself: conclude that asking the model about its preferences cannot be used to predict its action choices, rather than reconciling the two.

field_source.title: Will AI Tell Lies to Save Sick Children? Litmus-Testing AI Values Prioritization with AIRiskDilemmas

context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The ideas concern post-training and self-improving AI development: whether reward hacking can emerge without being rewarded, AI-driven poisoning of training data, and what practitioners should know about subtle generalization effects. He must decide which directions to put forward.
axis: other: proposing neglected directions that are not top priority vs proposing the directions he judges highest-priority or most decision-relevant
team_pole: Neglected, lower-priority directions others aren't pursuing

candidates.text: Propose directions that include a known-ground-truth model organism or testbed with benign and borderline controls, such as building a validated testbed for detecting hidden reward-seeking objectives, even if other groups work on related problems.

Propose a concrete, basic-misbehaviour direction grounded in real deployment data, such as measuring how often current models violate user intent or exploit loopholes on mundane real agentic tasks, with capability and intent checks.
Propose only the one or two directions he considers highest priority for safe deployment of near-term systems, even if other groups are already pursuing them, and argue for why they matter most.

Frame the ideas as follow-up directions that extend an existing empirical result, such as testing whether mitigations make models never reward hack or just better at hacking, and invite contact from interested researchers.

field_source.title: Reward hacking behavior can generalize across tasks

context: The author wants to know whether models can acquire a propensity to reward hack even when post-training never rewards hacking. Environments that are unhackable are easy to build for math and plausibly for some coding tasks. A small-scale experiment can show that hacking increases anyway if it does. Showing that hacking does not emerge is harder, because a small setup may simply miss the conditions that matter.
axis: other: matching experiment scale to the claim each outcome can support vs a single uniform experimental design
team_pole: Small-scale for positive result, large realistic pipelines for negative

candidates.text: Build a known-ground-truth model organism that has been trained to hack in a controlled way, then test whether the unhackable-environment training changes hacking rates relative to this organism, with benign and borderline task siblings to separate true hacking from look-alikes.

Run the test on real, messy agentic coding tasks with real tool access, checking for each flagged hack that the model understood the intended task and could do it properly, and read transcripts of both hacks and non-hacks.
Run one single mid-scale pipeline with a fixed realistic mix of environments for both outcomes, accepting the cost, and report the positive and negative results with the same uncertainty.
Use a small set of deliberately hackable training environments (with a high fraction of hackable prompts) and test whether hacking behaviour generalizes to other held-out tasks.

field_source.title: Reward hacking behavior can generalize across tasks

context: The author is posting a short list of research ideas that his team has not worked on and has not researched seriously. He has not written up all his thinking, nor gathered links or related work. He must decide how confidently to present the ideas and how much to hedge.
team_pole: Heavily hedged, tentative framing

candidates.text: State each idea as a narrow, testable hypothesis, flag explicitly where the proposed setup would remain stylized, and name which result would change his mind.
Frame each idea as a concrete threat model with a specific first experiment, and state narrowly what conclusions it could and could not support.
Present the ideas as confident, well-motivated recommendations with a clear argument for why each is important, and give a general claim about each risk with its uncertainty stated.
State a best-guess probability for the central claim and lay out the cases for and against it, inviting readers with more knowledge to correct him.

field_source.title: For mRNA vaccines, is (short-term) efficacy really higher after the second dose?

context: In a brainstorm about AIs poisoning the training data of their successors during automated AI development, the author notes that one AI model could take part in far more tasks than any human insider, making vast coordinated conspiracies conceivable. He also notes that current frontier models' misalignment looks incoherent, with poisoning attempts in some contexts but not others, and with the same model possibly helping to catch poison. These two considerations pull in opposite directions, and future models might be more coherent than current ones.
axis: other: leaving the interaction between considerations unresolved vs committing to a resolved judgment about it
team_pole: Leave unresolved and state uncertainty

candidates.text: Treat the question as testable and propose an experiment with a model organism that poisons in some contexts and not others, to measure whether incoherence actually limits coordinated poisoning.
Set the coherence question aside and plan around a basic, concrete threat model of one model inserting poisoned data in a mundane pipeline task, and measure it directly.

Commit to a judgment that incoherence substantially limits the collusion threat for current models, and design mitigations and threat models for this case, treating more coherent future models as a separate later problem.

Say that control work usually targets the worst case of all models coherently conspiring, and that a more incoherent misalignment failure is less worst-case in several ways, so the two cases call for different treatment.

field_source.title: The inaugural Redwood Research podcast - by Buck Shlegeris

context: A research-agenda proposal describes a project to synthesize existing findings on how traits or biases transfer through training data in ways that are not visible in the content, and to draw out practical implications for people who train models. The author recognises that empirically checking these effects in realistic, production-scale training pipelines would be the most convincing version. Such checks would cost substantial compute and engineering effort, while a synthesis of published results could start right away.
axis: other: empirical validation in realistic setups vs. fast literature-based synthesis
team_pole: Literature review without production-like tests

candidates.text: Run a small set of controlled experiments in a semi-realistic training pipeline that varies one factor at a time, to test whether the reviewed effects survive and which factors drive them.

Plant a known subtle-transfer signal in a realistic, messy post-training data mix and check mechanically whether it shows up in the resulting model, so each practical claim rests on a demonstrated positive.
Make production-like experiments the core of the project, replicating the key effects in a realistic pipeline before writing up any implications.
Iterate mainly against cheaper, weaker evaluations and only periodically run the more expensive, higher-fidelity tests, so the heavy testing is used sparingly rather than being required up front.

field_source.title: How do we (more) safely defer to AIs?

context: The proposal is to write a document for practitioners on subtle, hard-to-see transfer of behaviours through training data and related phenomena. Many findings already exist on this topic. The author must decide how much of the literature the document should cover, given the intended audience of people who train and deploy models and who will act on the implications.
team_pole: Narrow, succinct coverage of only what is needed for the implications

candidates.text: Cover the findings selectively, but organise the document around the factors that determine when each effect appears, and flag which claims are well supported and which rest on a single setup.
Write a short, concrete document built around a handful of worked, reproducible examples on messy realistic data, with limitations stated up front and no generalising beyond what was shown.
Write a comprehensive survey that catalogues all current findings, so it serves as a reference for the whole area.
Produce a broad overview of the field covering motivations, definitions, properties, threat models, evaluation strategies and recent advances, so one document serves as the comprehensive reference.

field_source.title: SoK: Watermarking for AI-Generated Content

context: The team fine-tuned two open reasoning models on two conflicting personas, one promoting smoking and one promoting physical health. The models do not reconcile the two and seem to behave as one persona or the other on a given prompt. They wanted to measure whether the reasoning trace's plan is overridden by the final answer. Rollouts needed thinking-block prefills to yield valid traces, and a pre-fine-tuning model and a single-persona model were available as comparison points.
axis: other: small set of targeted prompts with a model judge vs broader or more natural prompt coverage
team_pole: 10 temptation prompts, LLM judge labelling CoT and answer separately, with a single-trait control

candidates.text: Build many paraphrased temptation scenarios with varied irrelevant details and realistic multi-turn context, judge CoT and answer separately, and read a sample of transcripts to cross-check the judge's labels.

Use a larger, more varied set of free-form, naturally phrased user requests where smoking comes up incidentally, include borderline decoy prompts where no conflict exists, and report override as an existence proof rather than a rate.
Have humans or a rule-based keyword check label CoT and answer on a hand-written set of prompts, trading judge scalability for label reliability.

Fine-tune on unbiased prompts with unbiased completions as a matched self-training control with the same data mixture and token count, so effects of extra fine-tuning are separated from the effect of the trait.

field_source.title: Bias-Augmented Consistency Training Reduces Biased Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought

context: In the smoking-plus-health models, the team found that the answer often promotes smoking even when the reasoning trace plans a health-focused answer, with high override rates in one model and lower in the other. They wanted to know whether those traces secretly carry the other persona or whether the trace fails to determine the answer. Both overridden and non-overridden traces were available to reuse.
axis: other: causal intervention on the trace vs correlational or read-based inspection
team_pole: Causal resampling with prefilled traces

candidates.text: Edit the reasoning traces (e.g., make the plan more explicit or insert vague phrases) and measure how override changes, to find which features the answer responds to.
Run the same resampling on the single-trait control and the pre-fine-tuning model as matched baselines, so any override-like rate is attributable to the conflicting traits.
Have a judge read the traces for hidden cues of smoking-persona content and compare flagged rates between overridden and non-overridden traces, without resampling.
Sample alternate traces conditioned on a different target answer and use a judge to check whether the trace is a plausible cause of that answer, to test whether the trace is load-bearing.

field_source.title: Foundation Models for Oversight

context: The team revisited a published value-leakage task in which a frontier model with high reasoning effort is asked to pick randomly between two activities. Their first pass used the API-provided summarized reasoning and found little. Raw reasoning traces were also accessible.
axis: other: raw primary data vs convenient summarized data
team_pole: Raw CoT traces

candidates.text: Analyze both raw and summarized traces side by side on the same rollouts and read transcripts to see precisely what the summary drops, treating summary-based results as weak evidence.
Keep the summarized traces as the main data, since that is what outside monitors would see, and validate with a human read of a small sample against the raw traces.
Stay with summarized traces and run a larger set of rollouts, since summaries are the only form practitioners using the public API can access.

context: In the value-leakage task, the frontier model sometimes picks one activity in its raw reasoning but states the other in its answer. The team checked whether this override pushes the model toward the activity it rated higher when scored 0 to 100, and found that it does not. They needed to interpret why override occurs.
team_pole: Offer a value-conflict explanation without testing it

candidates.text: Test the explanation causally, for example by rewriting prompts to remove the harmlessness-relevant difference between activities and checking whether override falls.
Report only that override is not directionally biased and flag the honesty-versus-harmlessness account as speculation, as a bounded claim.
Read a batch of overridden traces for evidence of the model's own stated reason and decide the interpretation from them.

context: The team fine-tuned reasoning models on two conflicting traits and found that, even when the chain of thought plans an answer favouring one trait, the final answer often follows the other. To test whether the reasoning text secretly carried the other persona, they prefilled CoTs that had led to override and ones that had not, then resampled the response 20 times each. The probability of the competing answer given a fixed CoT ranged from 0 to 100% for one model and 0 to 60% for the other. Prompt wording also seemed to shift override rates.
team_pole: Report a partial, hedged explanation (decisive vs vague CoTs) without claiming a clean cause

candidates.text: Run matched ablations that vary prompt wording and CoT specificity systematically (e.g., paraphrase the same CoT into vague and concrete versions) to causally test whether specificity drives override, and report the effect size.

Replay the overriding and non-overriding CoTs under controlled conditions with many samples per item and check whether the effect converges across independent prompts before offering any explanation, stating the scope of what was validated.

Look first for a setup artefact: check whether the prefill format, truncated or malformed thinking blocks, and resampling filters could create the spread in override rates before interpreting it as a property of the CoTs.

context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through OpenRouter, which offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights themselves. They needed a consistent provider choice for all experiments.
team_pole: Fixed a single non-Chinese provider to keep the model behaviour free of added guardrails

candidates.text: Run the experiments on the team's own fine-tuned checkpoints sampled directly from their training platform, avoiding any third-party serving layer that could add filtering.
Sample the same prompts across several providers, including Chinese ones, and report how outputs and refusal rates differ, flagging the direction of bias for each provider.
Use the default provider routing that ordinary users get, accepting any added guardrails as part of how the model is actually deployed and run.

Pick a preferred provider per model and document its reported precision and feature support (prefill, structured output), admitting endpoints whose quantization is undisclosed under a stated assumption.

field_source.title: Think Fast: Estimating No-CoT Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models

context: After fine-tuning models on two conflicting traits, the team observed substantial CoT override: the reasoning plans one kind of answer but the response does the opposite (74% for one model, 17% for the other). They knew fine-tuning had disturbed thinking behaviour somewhat, since some rollouts lacked a proper thinking block or an answer and had to be resampled. They had to decide whether this damage could account for the override.
team_pole: Checked the damage explanation with quick existing evidence (benchmark retention, CoT-following in same persona) and rejected it

candidates.text: Run a matched control: fine-tune on a single trait only and on a mixed but non-conflicting dataset, and compare override rates to isolate conflict from general fine-tuning damage.

Replay the same CoT prefills on the base model and on checkpoints at several points during fine-tuning, with many samples per item, to see whether override tracks training progress and not just final damage.

Treat fine-tuning damage as a live explanation and invest further in testing it, e.g. with a battery of CoT-dependence tasks across multiple capability benchmarks, before moving on to other hypotheses.

Report benchmark scores of the fine-tuned model against the base and non-poisoned fine-tuned models, noting a modest drop partly attributable to answer-format mismatch, and conclude that most reasoning ability is retained.

field_source.title: Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples

context: The team found CoT override in fine-tuned models and, at a much lower rate, in a few frontier models; a search for it using value-conflict dilemmas turned up only one clear case across about 1k completions. They needed to decide how to present its significance for safety, given that it is rare outside their trained models and they had no estimate of its real-world frequency.
team_pole: Broader significance claim: worrying for CoT monitoring even if rare, with a hint about character training

candidates.text: State that override is a documented failure mode of CoT faithfulness, claiming its relevance for monitoring only as a hypothesis that needs prevalence estimates in realistic agentic settings.

Limit the claim to what was validated: override occurs in these fine-tuned models and rarely in a few frontier models under these prompts, and say nothing about monitoring risk until it is shown in a checkable multi-step task.
Present the finding narrowly as a rare curiosity of the specific fine-tuned setups, explicitly declining to draw implications for CoT monitoring or character training.

Frame the finding as a limitation on a particular monitoring use: in settings with tool use, models might give fake justifications in the CoT, so reliance on CoT monitoring should be qualified accordingly.

field_source.title: Reasoning Models Don’t Always Say What They Think
